entry.title: How quantum computers are being used for drug discovery

media:group.media:title: How quantum computers are being used for drug discovery
media:group.media:description:
It can take more than a decade for a medical discovery to become a drug doctors can prescribe.
You can read the full research here: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/cleveland-clinic-riken-chemistry
Researchers from @Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM are exploring how hybrid quantum-classical workflows could help accelerate this timeline–with exciting results.
Earlier this year, the collaboration successfully simulated the chemistry of two protein complexes with binding agents, T4-Lysozyme and Trypsin. The largest simulation of a Trypsin complex reached 12,635 atoms and more than 30,000 orbitals, earning the milestone of largest heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) electronic-structure calculation to date: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/cleveland-clinic-riken-chemistry
Recently nominated as a 2026 Gordon Bell finalist (https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/gordon-bell-finalists-2026), the work showed an improvement in accuracy by 210x within a key step of the workflow over previous approaches, attained through new algorithm developments and the close integration of QPUs, CPUs and GPUs.
In the latest entry of our research spotlight series, Dr. Kennie Merz. and Dr. Lara Jehi from Cleveland Clinic join IBM Quantum Head of Applied Quantum Science - Sarah Sheldon to explain how this deep integration of computing paradigms, known as quantum-centric supercomputing, helped achieve this remarkable moment in chemistry simulation at scale.

entry.title: How quantum computers tackle differential equations

media:group.media:title: How quantum computers tackle differential equations
media:group.media:description:
Some of the most important problems in science and engineering can be expressed using differential equations, which describe how systems change over time. From electrical circuits to fluid dynamics, plasma physics, and other complex natural phenomena, solving these equations often requires enormous computational resources. Researchers are increasingly exploring whether quantum computers can offer new ways of tackling these mathematical challenges.
In this episode of The Coherence Times, we’re joined by Duke University’s Di Fang and IBM Research’s Hari Krovi to explore the emerging field of quantum algorithms for differential equations. Together, they discuss how researchers develop new quantum algorithms, the evolution of approaches such as HHL, the challenges of running these methods on real quantum hardware, and what it will take for quantum computers to make an impact on scientific and engineering applications.

media:group.media:title: Inside quantum-centric supercomputing
media:group.media:description:
One of the biggest misconceptions about quantum computing is that it will eventually replace classical computing, but that’s not the case. *All* quantum computing relies on classical computing, even just for loading data and reading outputs, and many of the most promising quantum use cases involve quantum processing units (QPUs) working alongside the CPUs and GPUs behind powerful classical supercomputers. However, figuring out how these different computing paradigms fit together is easier said than done.
In this episode of The Coherence Times, we’re joined by IBM’s Seetharami Seelam and AMD’s Sanjay Chaurasia to explore the emerging world of quantum-centric supercomputing. Together, they discuss the similarities and differences between GPUs and QPUs, explain how quantum and classical systems work together, and offer a glimpse at the next generation of hybrid computing.

entry.title: A day in the life of a Cryogenic Systems Engineer

media:group.media:title: A day in the life of a Cryogenic Systems Engineer
media:group.media:description:
In August 2026, IBM successfully connected and cooled two cryogenic modules into a single operating environment: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/modular-cryogenics
The achievement validates a fundamental design principle behind the IBM Quantum roadmap: Quantum computers of the future should be built as modular systems.
Instead of housing processors inside isolated cryostats, our architecture creates connected cryogenic cells that can be linked together while maintaining the ultra-cold temperatures required for quantum computation.
In this video, IBM Quantum Cryogenic Assembly Engineer Allie Lindler answers some of our most frequently asked questions about this new modular approach to housing and cooling quantum processors, including what it takes to achieve and maintain scalable, ultracold temperatures as a cryogenics specialist.

media:group.media:title: Inside quantum optimization research
media:group.media:description:
Optimization is often cited as one of quantum computing’s most promising applications. Businesses and researchers are constantly searching for better routes, schedules, allocations, and ways to allocate limited resources, meaning that a computational advantage for quantum optimization methods could deliver enormous value. Yet despite years of research, fundamental questions remain: Which optimization problems are best suited to quantum computers? And how will we know when quantum methods have truly surpassed their classical counterparts?
In this episode of the Coherence Times, we’re joined by IBM’s Stefan Wörner and Stephanie Riedmüller of the Zuse Institute to explore the promise and limitations of quantum optimization. Together, they discuss the search for new quantum algorithms, the importance of benchmarking and community-driven research, and what it will take for quantum computers to deliver practical advantages for real-world optimization problems.
Learn more about quantum computing and explore the IBM Quantum Platform → https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com
Are you an optimization researcher? Contribute to the Quantum Optimization Benchmarking Library → https://github.com/ZIB-AOPT/QOBLIB

entry.title: How to install a quantum computer

media:group.media:title: How to install a quantum computer
media:group.media:description:
Quantum computers represent a fundamentally new paradigm in the science of computation, so it’s no surprise that quantum system installations are anything but ordinary. From cryogenic cooling to complex control electronics, deploying a quantum computer requires specialized infrastructure and expertise.
In this episode of The Coherence Times, we sit down with John Kolb of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and IBM’s Rajeev Malik to go behind the scenes of a unique installation: a quantum computer housed inside a restored chapel. Together, they offerrare insight into what it takes to install and operate quantum systems, how quantum fits alongside classical supercomputing, and what the future of quantum-centric supercomputing could look like as the technology scales.
Visit IBM Quantum Platform to run circuits on real quantum hardware: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com

entry.title: Why IBM quantum computers are colder than space

media:group.media:title: Why IBM quantum computers are colder than space
media:group.media:description:
IBM’s superconducting quantum computers don’t just require advanced quantum processors, they also rely on highly specialized systems to keep those processors operating in an environment that is stable, protected, and colder than the furthest reaches of outer space. As quantum computers scale, the infrastructure that houses, cools, and operates them must advance as well—delivering systems that are easier to maintain, upgrade, and link with other systems.
In this episode of The Coherence Times, we’re joined by IBM’s Matt Hollister and Allie Lindler to dive deeper into the advanced cooling technology that makes superconducting quantum computing possible. Together, they discuss why cryogenic hardware matters, what goes into engineering refrigeration systems for the for modular quantum systems of the future, and how a new modular platform could help support the next generation quantum processors and systems.

entry.title: Unveiling IBM's cryogenic modules to scale fault-tolerant quantum computing

media:group.media:title: Unveiling IBM's cryogenic modules to scale fault-tolerant quantum computing
media:group.media:description:
IBM has successfully linked and cooled down the first operational modules of a scalable cryogenic system designed to support its fault-tolerant quantum computing mission. Connected together at an IBM Quantum facility in New York, the quantum fridges form IBM's first realization of the modular, shared, and ultra-cold environment required to operate multiple quantum processors. This milestone advances IBM's path to building IBM Quantum Starling, which is expected to be the world's first fault-tolerant quantum computer.
Learn more at: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog

media:group.media:title: How quantum computers model molecules
media:group.media:description:
Visit The Coherence Times podcast page to get more quantum content → https://www.ibm.com/think/podcasts/the-coherence-times
The very first proposals for quantum computing centered on its potential to simulate molecules and other quantum systems—a task that is still considered one of the technology’s most promising applications today. However, scaling these simulations to real-world use cases remains a major challenge. In this episode of The Coherence Times, we sit down with Cleveland Clinic’s Dr. Kennie Merz and IBM's Dr. Jamie Garcia to explore a new milestone in the field: the simulation of a protein with more than 12,000 atoms using state-of-the-art quantum–classical techniques. Together, they discuss why chemistry is such a natural fit for quantum computers, how researchers are simulating increasingly complex molecules on today’s quantum hardware, and what it will take to move from early demonstrations to practical applications in areas like drug discovery and materials science.
Learn more about Cleveland Clinic’s large-scale protein simulation work with IBM: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/cleveland-clinic-riken-chemistry
Explore the simulation method for yourself with our tutorial on IBM Quantum Platform: https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/tutorials/sample-based-quantum-diagonalization

entry.title: Building time crystals with quantum computers

media:group.media:title: Building time crystals with quantum computers
media:group.media:description:
Crystals are defined by repeating patterns—but what if those patterns unfold in time rather than space? In this episode of The Coherence Times, we take a closer look at “time crystals”—systems of interacting particles that exhibit unique behaviors when driven by regular pulses of energy.
Join host Ryan Mandelbaum as they speak with Dr. Eric Switzer and Dr. Nicolás Lorente, two researchers who recently used IBM’s quantum computers to create and study a two-dimensional time crystal. Together, they break down what it means for a system to behave like a crystal in time, why studying systems out of equilibrium matters, and how quantum computers enable experiments that go beyond the limitations of purely classical methods. entry.title: A decade of quantum on the cloud

media:group.media:title: A decade of quantum on the cloud
media:group.media:description:
Visit The Coherence Times podcast page to get more AI content → https://www.ibm.com/think/podcasts/the-coherence-times
It was almost exactly ten years ago, on May 4, 2026, that IBM put the first quantum computer on the cloud. This was a seminal moment in computing history. For the first time, anyone could run quantum circuits on a real quantum computer from anywhere with an internet connection. That single act took quantum computers out of the research lab, and put them in the hands of a global community of researchers, developers, students, and enthusiasts. In this week’s episode of The Coherence Times, we sit down with IBM Quantum CTO of Quantum-Centric Supercomputing Jerry Chow and Oak Ridge National Laboratory Quantum Science Center Director Travis Humble to discuss that moment in history, and the decade of exploration and ecosystem development it inspired.
